title: Concept Drills — d- and f-Block / Coordination Chemistry (Class 12 Chemistry)
subject: chemistry

questions.concept: Variable oxidation states — why d-block differs
questions.question: Why do transition metals show several oxidation states (Mn: +2 to +7) while Ca is stuck at +2?
questions.solution: Transition metals have (n−1)d and ns electrons of similar energy, so varying numbers of BOTH can participate in bonding — each successive ionisation removes a d electron at modest extra cost, giving a ladder of stable states. Ca has only ns² valence electrons; removing the third (from a core shell) costs far too much energy. The near-degeneracy of (n−1)d and ns is the root cause.

questions.question: Why are [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ blue but [Zn(H₂O)₆]²⁺ colourless, even though both are aqua complexes?
questions.solution: Cu²⁺ is d⁹ — a partially filled d set lets an electron absorb visible light and jump between split d orbitals (d–d transition); the complement colour is seen. Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰ — the d set is full, so no d–d transition is possible and all visible light passes through. A partially filled d subshell is the colour requirement.

questions.question: Define lanthanoid contraction, state its cause, and give two consequences (one in the lanthanoids, one in the following elements).
questions.solution: The steady decrease in atomic/ionic radii across the lanthanoid series (Ce → Lu). Cause: the added electrons fill the poorly-shielding 4f subshell, so each proton added pulls the shell in without f-electrons screening effectively. Consequences: (1) lanthanoids become so similar in size that their separation is difficult; (2) the 5d transition metals after them (Zr/Hf) have nearly identical radii — hence near-identical chemistry and hard separation.

questions.question: Why do transition metals and their compounds make good catalysts (Fe in Haber, V₂O₅ in contact process)? Give the two properties involved.
questions.solution: (1) Variable oxidation states let them form transient intermediate compounds, lowering activation energy by providing an alternative path. (2) Large surface area with vacant d orbitals lets them ADSORB reactant molecules onto the surface, orienting and weakening their bonds. Both properties come from the incompletely filled d subshell.

questions.question: Why are transition metals hard and high-melting, and why does adding a small amount of carbon to iron transform its properties?
questions.solution: Many valence electrons in metallic bonding plus small atoms occupying INTERSTITIAL sites between the large metal atoms give strong, non-directional multi-centre bonding — hence hardness and high melting points. Carbon in iron's interstices (steel) pins dislocations and distorts the lattice, so the metal resists deformation — a few percent C changes mechanical behaviour dramatically.

questions.concept: Werner's theory — primary and secondary valence
questions.question: In [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃, which ligands satisfy primary valence and which secondary? State what each corresponds to in modern terms.
questions.solution: Primary valence = ionisable: the 3 Cl⁻, satisfied by the Co³⁺ charge — they precipitate with AgNO₃ and correspond to OXIDATION STATE. Secondary valence = coordination: the 6 NH₃, non-ionisable, fixed in number and geometry — corresponds to COORDINATION NUMBER (6, octahedral). The two valences are independent, which is why [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ and [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl both exist.

questions.question: Why is [Ni(en)₃]²⁺ far more stable than [Ni(NH₃)₆]²⁺, though both bind nitrogen donors?
questions.solution: en (ethylenediamine) is BIDENTATE: each molecule attaches at two points, forming five-membered chelate rings. Replacing one chelated ligand requires breaking TWO coordinate bonds simultaneously and the ring geometry resists it — statistically and energetically disfavoured. More chelate rings → greater stability (the chelate effect); entropy also favours it since particles increase on dissociation.

questions.concept: Ligand strength in the spectrochemical series
questions.question: Why is [CoF₆]³⁻ paramagnetic with a different colour from [Co(CN)₆]³⁻, which is diamagnetic?
questions.solution: F⁻ is a WEAK-field ligand: small Δ₀ means pairing costs more than promoting an electron, so electrons stay unpaired (high-spin, paramagnetic). CN⁻ is STRONG-field: large Δ₀ forces pairing (low-spin, diamagnetic). The ligand's position in the spectrochemical series sets Δ₀, which sets the spin state — and the colour, since Δ₀ is the absorbed photon energy.
